assumptions: This is a prospective delivery risk register, not a report of observed defects, shipped mitigations, tested outcomes, or a production environment.
The approved requirements_analysis output supplies the only linked identifiers, REQ-001 through REQ-021; no stage_output locator was supplied, so no stage_output reference is invented.
The must and should priority values express qualitative attention to delivery risks, not requirement priority, measured likelihood, or an approved severity scale.

Known-account requests are checked against the five-per-account-per-hour limit without assuming a limit for unknown accounts; the reset-request response must not disclose account existence, including when considering throttling.
Active sessions means sessions represented by the application for an account; the session mechanism remains unspecified.

The sign-in button is a visible control without an inferred authentication outcome. New-password policy, reset-link transport, persistence across restart, and recovery-page visual layout remain unspecified.
Notifications are observed in the in-memory sink, not presumed to be externally delivered; accounts used for this small application are synthetic.

open_questions.question: How should requests for nonexistent accounts count toward an hourly per-account limit?
open_questions.context: Relevant to R22A08-003 and R22A08-004; do not invent an unknown-account threshold, and keep responses independent of account existence.

open_questions.question: What response should a throttled request produce, and how will it avoid distinguishing existing from nonexistent accounts?
open_questions.context: Relevant to R22A08-003 and R22A08-004; the exact throttled response is not specified.

open_questions.question: How will the application represent all active sessions of one account?
open_questions.context: Relevant to R22A08-007; check invalidation of every represented session without prescribing the mechanism.

open_questions.question: Is the visible Sign in button intended to authenticate, and what outcome, if any, should it have?
open_questions.context: Relevant to R22A08-001; only the displayed control is specified.

open_questions.question: What new-password policy, if any, should be applied?
open_questions.context: Relevant to R22A08-006; no length or complexity rule is inferred.

open_questions.question: How should reset links be conveyed to owners?
open_questions.context: Relevant to R22A08-005 and R22A08-008; the in-memory sink is observable, but external delivery is not prescribed.

open_questions.question: Should synthetic account, link, session, or notification state survive an application restart?
open_questions.context: Relevant to R22A08-006 through R22A08-008; restart persistence is not required by the available evidence.

open_questions.question: What should the recovery-request and new-password pages look like?
open_questions.context: Relevant to R22A08-002; the supplied wireframe shows only the sign-in page.

summary: Ten prospective delivery risks cover the approved REQ-001 through REQ-021 for a small Python 3.12 Flask password-reset application. Checks are proposed, not claimed as implemented; no deployment or deployment workflow is in scope.

sections.heading: Purpose and interpretation
sections.body: Each risk describes a possible cause and impact followed by a practical proposed mitigation/check. Requirement links use approved requirements_analysis IDs only. Must marks the most consequential recovery-flow and account-protection risks for attention; should marks important presentation, verification, and delivery-boundary risks. Neither value changes a requirement's status, establishes a likelihood measurement, or asserts an existing defect.

sections.heading: Evidence and scope
sections.body: The story defines a Python 3.12 Flask server-rendered pytest application with synthetic accounts, an in-memory notification sink, production-limitations documentation, and no deployment or deployment workflows. The attachment shows only the sign-in page. The run-specific recovery standard defines account-independent reset-request responses, at most five requests per account per hour, single-use links expiring 30 minutes after issuance, sign-out of all active sessions on successful reset, and owner notification after every successful reset. There is no supplied implementation, test outcome, production architecture, or reset-page design.

items.title: Sign-in presentation or server rendering diverges from the wireframe
items.description: Cause: The server-rendered sign-in template or input markup could omit or alter the centered outlined white card, “Sign in” heading, labeled “Email address” field with name@example.com placeholder, labeled masked “Password” field with asterisks, dark rectangular “Sign in” button, or “No account? Contact your administrator.” footer. Impact: The supplied sign-in experience and specified page behavior would not be represented accurately. Proposed mitigation/check: Compare the rendered page with the observed wireframe, inspect field labels and masking, and exercise server-rendered output. Do not infer that the visible button performs authentication.

items.title: Forgot-password entry does not start recovery
items.description: Cause: The blue underlined “Forgot password?” link could be missing, hard to recognize, or not connected to a server-rendered reset-request flow. Impact: A user could not begin recovery from the supplied sign-in page. Proposed mitigation/check: Inspect the visible link and follow it from the sign-in page to a functional reset-request entry, checking that page content is server-rendered; do not invent a visual design for recovery pages.

items.title: Reset-request responses disclose account existence
items.description: Cause: Conditional response content or status for an existing versus nonexistent account, including behavior around throttling, could differ. Impact: Reset requests could reveal whether a synthetic account exists, contrary to the recovery standard. Proposed mitigation/check: Compare otherwise equivalent reset-request responses for known and unknown identifiers and inspect throttled cases for disclosure; the exact throttled response and unknown-account counting remain open, not presumed to be implemented.

items.title: Known-account hourly reset-request limit is exceeded
items.description: Cause: Request counting, time-window boundaries, or inconsistent throttling could allow more than five accepted reset requests for one known account within an hour, or make account existence apparent. Impact: The volume control or response indistinguishability could fail. Proposed mitigation/check: Submit six requests for a known account within one hour, verify no more than five are accepted, check a window boundary, and compare responses so throttling does not reveal account existence. Unknown-account counting and the precise throttled response remain undecided.

items.title: Reset link remains usable after consumption or expiry
items.description: Cause: Link state might not be consumed on successful use, or expiry might be computed from a later event or checked with the wrong 30-minute boundary. Impact: A replayed or expired link could complete another password reset. Proposed mitigation/check: Use a valid link once and attempt replay; attempt use just before, exactly at, and after 30 minutes from issuance, confirming that the link cannot complete a reset at or after the boundary. Reset-link transport is unspecified.

items.title: Successful reset fails to change a synthetic account password
items.description: Cause: Completion could neglect the linked account state, or fixtures could accidentally rely on real identities instead of synthetic accounts. Impact: A valid unused unexpired link would not produce the intended password change, or the synthetic-only boundary could be lost. Proposed mitigation/check: Exercise a complete reset against a synthetic fixture and inspect the account password state before and after; inspect account data for synthetic-only identities. No new-password policy or restart-persistence guarantee is inferred.

items.title: A successful reset leaves an active session signed in
items.description: Cause: Reset completion could invalidate only the current session or omit other application-represented active sessions for the account. Impact: A pre-reset signed-in session could remain usable despite a successful reset. Proposed mitigation/check: Establish multiple represented active sessions for one synthetic account, complete its reset, and confirm none remains signed in. The session mechanism and definition of active beyond application representation remain open.

items.title: Owner notification is missed or leaves the in-memory sink
items.description: Cause: The success path could omit a notification, address the wrong owner, or use an external delivery path instead of the in-memory sink. Impact: A successful reset would not produce the specified observable owner notice or would exceed the small-app delivery boundary. Proposed mitigation/check: For every successful reset in the test scenarios, inspect the in-memory sink for an owner-addressed notification recorded after completion and verify notifications are captured there rather than externally delivered. No external link transport is assumed.

items.title: Runtime or pytest coverage diverges from the requested delivery
items.description: Cause: Implementation could target a different Python runtime or framework, or automated tests could omit sign-in or recovery behaviors. Impact: The delivered project might not be verifiable against its specified technical and behavioral constraints. Proposed mitigation/check: Inspect the configured Python 3.12 runtime and Flask usage; run pytest and inspect test cases for the sign-in presentation and recovery request, limit, link, completion, sessions, and notifications. No implementation or test results are available at this risk-assessment stage.

items.title: Production limitations or no-deployment boundary are missed
items.description: Cause: Documentation could omit the small application's production limitations, or delivery work could deploy it or add a deployment workflow despite the explicit boundary. Impact: Readers might mistake the demo for a production-ready service, or delivery could exceed approved scope. Proposed mitigation/check: Review project documentation for production limitations and review delivery actions and changed workflow files to verify there was no deployment and no new deployment workflow. This does not propose deployment.
